facts.claim: The Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional in Brown v. Board of Education
facts.context: Decided unanimously in May 1954, overturning the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
facts.goDeeper: The ruling did not set a deadline, and many districts resisted for more than a decade.

facts.claim: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, starting the Montgomery bus boycott
facts.context: Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955; the boycott began four days later.
facts.goDeeper: She was a trained NAACP secretary, not a woman who happened to be tired. The act was deliberate.

facts.claim: Days the Montgomery bus boycott lasted
facts.context: It ran for 381 days, ending in December 1956 after the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation.
facts.goDeeper: Around 40,000 Black commuters walked, carpooled or took Black-owned taxis for over a year.

facts.claim: The Little Rock Nine desegregated Central High School under federal escort
facts.context: Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne to Arkansas in September 1957 to enforce the court order.
facts.goDeeper: The governor had used the National Guard to block the students. The president federalised it and sent it home.

facts.claim: Four students began the Greensboro lunch counter sit-in
facts.context: On 1 February 1960 four Black college students sat at a whites-only Woolworth's counter and refused to leave.
facts.goDeeper: Within two months sit-ins had spread to more than 50 cities across nine states.

facts.claim: The Freedom Rides tested desegregation on interstate buses
facts.context: Integrated groups rode buses into the South in 1961 to test rulings that were being ignored.
facts.goDeeper: A bus was firebombed in Anniston, Alabama, and riders were beaten while police stayed away.

facts.claim: The Birmingham campaign brought police dogs and fire hoses onto national television
facts.context: Spring 1963 protests met with dogs and high-pressure hoses, including against schoolchildren.
facts.goDeeper: The images shifted national opinion sharply and helped force the Civil Rights Act through Congress.

facts.claim: King wrote his Letter from Birmingham Jail
facts.context: Written in April 1963 in response to white clergymen who called the protests unwise and untimely.
facts.goDeeper: He began it in the margins of a newspaper, having no writing paper in the cell.

facts.claim: Marchers were attacked crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge on Bloody Sunday
facts.context: State troopers assaulted marchers leaving Selma on 7 March 1965.
facts.goDeeper: The Voting Rights Act was signed five months later.

facts.claim: Distance of the Selma to Montgomery march
facts.context: About 54 miles along Highway 80, completed on the third attempt over five days.
facts.goDeeper: The final march was federally protected, and around 25,000 people arrived at the state capitol.

facts.claim: The Fair Housing Act banned discrimination in the sale and rental of housing
facts.context: Signed in April 1968, a week after King's assassination.
facts.goDeeper: It had been stalled in Congress for two years. His death broke the deadlock.

facts.claim: The Supreme Court struck down bans on interracial marriage in Loving v. Virginia
facts.context: The unanimous ruling invalidated such laws in the sixteen states that still had them.
facts.goDeeper: Richard and Mildred Loving had been sentenced to a year in prison, suspended on condition they leave Virginia.

facts.claim: Martin Luther King Jr. received the Nobel Peace Prize
facts.context: Awarded at 35, making him the youngest recipient at that time.
facts.goDeeper: He gave the entire prize money, about $54,000, to the movement.

facts.claim: Martin Luther King Jr.'s age when he was killed
facts.context: He was 39, having led the movement nationally for twelve years since Montgomery.
facts.goDeeper: He was 26 when the bus boycott began.

facts.claim: Martin Luther King Jr. Day was first observed as a federal holiday
facts.context: Signed into law in 1983 and first observed in January 1986.
facts.goDeeper: It was not observed in all fifty states until 2000.

facts.claim: Rosa Parks was the first person arrested for refusing to give up a bus seat in Montgomery
facts.context: Claudette Colvin, aged 15, was arrested for the same act nine months earlier. Organisers chose Parks as the test case.
facts.goDeeper: Colvin was one of four plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the case that actually ended bus segregation.

facts.claim: The most famous passage of the 'I Have a Dream' speech was not in the prepared text
facts.context: King had used the dream passage before and cut it from the draft. He returned to it from memory at the podium.
facts.goDeeper: Mahalia Jackson called out 'Tell them about the dream, Martin' from behind him.

facts.claim: The movement was united behind nonviolent tactics
facts.context: Nonviolence was central to King and the SCLC, but figures such as Malcolm X and later the Black Panthers argued for self-defence and different aims.
facts.goDeeper: The disagreement was strategic and public, and it sharpened after 1965.

facts.claim: Women organised much of the movement's day-to-day work
facts.context: Ella Baker, Septima Clark, Diane Nash, Jo Ann Robinson and Fannie Lou Hamer were central to organising and strategy.
facts.goDeeper: Robinson mimeographed 35,000 leaflets overnight to launch the Montgomery boycott.

facts.claim: The FBI conducted surveillance of Martin Luther King Jr.
facts.context: The Bureau wiretapped him for years and sent an anonymous letter urging him to kill himself.
facts.goDeeper: The Church Committee documented this in 1975, and the surveillance tapes are sealed until 2027.
